evidence.excerpt:
We present YOLO, a new approach to object detection.
Prior work on object detection repurposes classifiers to per-
form detection. Instead, we frame object detection as a re-
gression problem to spatially separated bounding boxes and
associated class probabilities. A single neural network pre-
dicts bounding boxes and class probabilities directly from
full images in one evaluation. Since the whole detection
pipeline is a single network, it can be optimized end-to-end
directly on detection performance.
Our unified architecture is extremely fast. Our base
YOLO model processes images in real-time at 45 frames
per second. A smaller version of the network, Fast YOLO,
processes an astounding 155 frames per second while
still achieving double the mAP of other real-time detec-
tors. Compared to state-of-the-art detection systems, YOLO
makes more localization errors but is less likely to

evidence.excerpt:
We unify the separate components of object detection
into a single neural network. Our network uses features
from the entire image to predict each bounding box. It also
predicts all bounding boxes across all classes for an im-
age simultaneously. This means our network reasons glob-
ally about the full image and all the objects in the image.
The YOLO design enables end-to-end training and real-
time speeds while maintaining high average precision.
Our system divides the input image into an S×S grid.
If the center of an object falls into a grid cell, that grid cell
is responsible for detecting that object.
Each grid cell predictsB bounding boxes and confidence
scores for those boxes. These confidence scores reflect how
confident the model is that the box contains an object and
also how accurate it thinks the box is that it predicts. For-
mally we define confidence as Pr(Object)∗

evidence.excerpt:
YOLO imposes strong spatial constraints on bounding
box predictions since each grid cell only predicts two boxes
and can only have one class. This spatial constraint lim-
its the number of nearby objects that our model can pre-
dict. Our model struggles with small objects that appear in
groups, such as flocks of birds.
Since our model learns to predict bounding boxes from
data, it struggles to generalize to objects in new or unusual
aspect ratios or configurations. Our model also uses rela-
tively coarse features for predicting bounding boxes since
our architecture has multiple downsampling layers from the
input image.
Finally, while we train on a loss function that approxi-
mates detection performance, our loss function treats errors
the same in small bounding boxes versus large bounding
boxes. A small error in a large box is generally benign but a

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Final evaluation uses standard mAP on held-out PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 test sets and cross-domain artwork datasets, which are external benchmark protocols independent of the training loss.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Mean average precision (mAP) on PASCAL VOC 2007/2012 test sets and cross-domain artwork datasets.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: End-to-end supervised training with a multi-part sum-squared error loss over bounding box coordinates, IoU confidence, and class probabilities against ground-truth annotations.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: Reported inference speeds (45 fps base, 155 fps Fast YOLO) and accuracy figures (63.4% and 52.7% mAP on VOC 2007) are well supported by the experimental data, with candid acknowledgement of higher localization errors relative to two-stage systems.
primary.evaluation_assessment: The model is rigorously evaluated on standard benchmarks including PASCAL VOC 2007 and 2012, as well as cross-domain artwork datasets, comparing both mean average precision (mAP) and frame rates against prior real-time and region-proposal methods.

evaluation_independence.corroboration_summary: Final evaluation relies on external benchmark protocols and test sets measured by standard mAP, independent of the multi-term loss used during training.
evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Mean average precision (mAP) computed against held-out ground truth annotations on standard test sets (PASCAL VOC 2007/2012, Picasso, and People-Art).
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: End-to-end supervised training using sum-squared error over bounding box coordinates, IoU confidence predictions, and conditional class probabilities against ground-truth annotations.

primary.limitations: The authors document key spatial constraints of the grid, difficulty detecting small or clustered objects, struggles with unusual aspect ratios, and inferior localization accuracy compared to leading multi-stage detectors.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology divides input images into an S x S grid where each cell predicts bounding boxes, confidence values, and class probabilities in a single forward pass, optimized via a multi-part sum-squared error loss function.
primary.quality_rationale: The manuscript presents an influential, thoroughly detailed architecture with extensive quantitative evaluations across speed, accuracy, error profiles, and out-of-domain generalization.
primary.scoped_contribution: The paper introduces YOLO, framing object detection as a single end-to-end regression neural network that maps full images directly to bounding box coordinates and class probabilities, achieving real-time inference speed.

scholarly_quality.rationale: The manuscript presents an influential, thoroughly detailed architecture with extensive quantitative evaluations across speed, accuracy, error profiles, and out-of-domain generalization.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors document key spatial constraints of the grid, difficulty detecting small or clustered objects, struggles with unusual aspect ratios, and inferior localization accuracy compared to leading multi-stage detectors.
